prompt: Why does a stream's compute cost not fall on a quiet Tuesday night?

choices.text: Kafka processes old messages again while it is idle
choices.why: An idle broker does almost nothing; the cost is that it is there.

choices.text: The brokers and consumers run all the time, ready for the next sale
choices.why: Right: sized for the peak, paid at the trough.

choices.text: Compression costs more at night
choices.why: Nothing about compression depends on the hour.

choices.text: Retention is counted in hours of traffic
choices.why: Retention is time on disk, whatever the traffic.

prompt: A topic is written at 2 MB/s, has three replicas, and five consumer groups read all of it. How many MB/s move in total: in, between brokers, and out?
hint: In once, to every follower, out once per group.

prompt: A cluster spans three availability zones for safety. Which traffic is most likely to show up on the network bill?

choices.text: Replica copies and consumer reads that cross a zone boundary
choices.why: Right: two of every three copies cross one, and so do remote reads.

choices.text: Heartbeats between consumers and the coordinator
choices.why: They exist, but they are tiny next to the data.

choices.text: Writes from a producer to a leader in its own zone
choices.why: Traffic inside a zone is the part not usually billed.

choices.text: Reading the index files
choices.why: Index reads stay on the broker's own disk.

prompt: The JSON of one sale is about 122 bytes, yet the topic holds about 135 bytes per sale. Where does the difference come from?

choices.text: The index files beside the log
choices.why: `kafka-log-dirs.sh` counted the `.log` file alone.

choices.text: Replication: the second copy
choices.why: One node, one copy; replication multiplies it later.

choices.text: The key, and the record's and batch's own fields
choices.why: Right: offset, timestamp, framing, the batch header.

choices.text: Kafka pads every message to a fixed size
choices.why: Records are variable length; nothing is padded.

prompt: The `.index` file of a live segment is 10 485 760 bytes. Why is that not part of the bytes per sale?

choices.text: It is compressed
choices.why: It is not; it is preallocated.

choices.text: It belongs to another topic
choices.why: It sits in the same partition directory.

choices.text: It holds the consumer offsets
choices.why: Those live in `__consumer_offsets`.

choices.text: It is preallocated and trimmed when the segment closes
choices.why: Right: on a live segment its size says little.

prompt: A till that sends one sale every few seconds writes to a topic. Compared with the 100 000 sales sent at full speed, what happens to the bytes per sale?

choices.text: They fall, since there is less traffic
choices.why: Less traffic means smaller batches, which cost more per message.

choices.text: They rise: each sale pays a batch header of its own
choices.why: Right: the measurement depended on full batches.

choices.text: They stay the same, because the message is the same
choices.why: The message is the same; the batching around it is not.

choices.text: They double, because of replication
choices.why: Replication multiplies copies, not the size of one.

prompt: Why do Ponto Final's JSON sales compress so well?

choices.text: Every batch repeats the same field names and a few values
choices.why: Right: five shops, eight books, the same five keys.

choices.text: JSON is already a binary format
choices.why: It is text, which is why it compresses.

choices.text: Kafka removes duplicate sales
choices.why: Nothing is removed; repetition inside a batch is stored once.

choices.text: Each message is compressed on its own
choices.why: Kafka compresses a batch at a time, which is why repetition across sales helps.

prompt: In this lab, which codec gave the smallest topic for the 100 000 sales?

choices.text: `zstd`
choices.why: Close, at 16.9 bytes a sale, but not the smallest here.

choices.text: `lz4`
choices.why: 31.5 bytes a sale, about a quarter of uncompressed.

choices.text: `uncompressed`
choices.why: 135.3 bytes a sale, the largest.

choices.text: `gzip`
choices.why: Right: 14.5 bytes a sale on these sales.

prompt: `gzip` was smallest in the lab. Why might a new pipeline still choose `zstd` on the producer?

choices.text: `gzip` is not allowed on a producer
choices.why: Every codec is available on the producer.

choices.text: A close ratio for far less processor time
choices.why: Right: size is one half of the trade, CPU the other.

choices.text: `zstd` needs no decompression by consumers
choices.why: Every consumer group decompresses whatever the codec.

choices.text: `gzip` corrupts JSON
choices.why: Compression is lossless; the sales come back byte for byte.

prompt: On a topic, the `compression.type` value that keeps whatever the producer sent is ___.
A topic receives 1 000 000 messages a day of 50 bytes each on disk, kept 10 days with 3 copies. How many gigabytes (10^9 bytes) does it hold in all copies?
What did `bill.py` say a week of Ponto Final's sales needs, in all three copies?

choices.text: About 7 MB
choices.why: Right: 7.1 MB, a memory card's worth.

choices.text: About 7 GB
choices.why: A thousand times too much: check the units.

choices.text: About 420 GB
choices.why: That was the clickstream example.

choices.text: About 372 MB
choices.why: That was a year of retention.

prompt: Retention is 7 days and segments are 1 GB, but a quiet partition holds 9 days of messages. Why?

choices.text: The broker ignores retention on quiet topics
choices.why: Retention applies; it just applies to whole segments.

choices.text: Retention is counted from the last consumer read
choices.why: Reading has nothing to do with deletion.

choices.text: A segment is deleted only once its newest message is past the limit
choices.why: Right: deletion is per segment, so old messages wait for their segment.

choices.text: Compaction keeps the extra days
choices.why: This topic deletes; nothing compacts it.

prompt: Match each lever to what pulling it costs.

pairs.right: replays cannot reach as far back
processor time on producers and consumers

prompt: Why can the sales topic not be compacted, when a stock-per-book topic can?

choices.text: Sales have no key
choices.why: They do: the shop. The problem is what the key would mean.

choices.text: Each sale is a fact of its own; keeping one per key would lose the rest
choices.why: Right: compaction suits state, not history.

choices.text: Compaction only works on one partition
choices.why: It works on any number of partitions.

choices.text: Compacted topics cannot be read by consumers
choices.why: They are read like any other topic.

prompt: A topic keeps a year of events, and almost nobody reads anything older than a week. What does tiered storage change?

choices.text: The old segments move to cheaper object storage
choices.why: Right: the largest line of the bill moves to the cheapest storage.

choices.text: Old events are deleted after a week
choices.why: They are kept, elsewhere; `retention.ms` still covers the year.

choices.text: Old events are compacted to one per key
choices.why: That is compaction, a different arrangement.

choices.text: Every read becomes faster
choices.why: Reads of the old part become slower, from the object store.

prompt: A message with a key and no value, which tells a compacted topic to forget that key, is called a ___.
A managed service bills throughput out per byte. What multiplies that line for one topic?

choices.text: The number of consumer groups reading it
choices.why: Right: every group reads the whole topic.

choices.text: The number of partitions
choices.why: Partitions split the bytes; they do not multiply them.

choices.text: The retention
choices.why: Retention is the storage line.

choices.text: The compression codec
choices.why: Compression divides, it does not multiply.

prompt: Under a model that charges per partition hour, a team creates 100 partitions "for later" on a quiet topic. What is wrong with that?

choices.text: Kafka refuses more than 50 partitions
choices.why: It allows far more; the issue is the bill.

choices.text: Partitions can never be added later
choices.why: They can; adding moves keys, as lesson 3 warns, but it is possible.

choices.text: Each idle partition is billed every hour from today
choices.why: Right: the price is paid before the need arrives.

choices.text: Consumers read faster from many partitions
choices.why: Only up to one consumer per partition, and the topic is quiet.

prompt: In the lab, how did the idle broker's memory behave over a minute with nothing written?

choices.text: It dropped to almost nothing
choices.why: It stayed over half a gigabyte.

choices.text: It stayed above half a gigabyte
choices.why: Right: the heap is reserved while the node runs.

choices.text: It grew to several gigabytes
choices.why: It stayed near 540 MB.

choices.text: It was released to the operating system
choices.why: Nothing was returned; the node holds its heap.

prompt: Which of Ponto Final's needs is the lesson's best case for a stream rather than a batch?

choices.text: The monthly sales report
choices.why: Read later: a nightly batch serves it for twenty minutes.

choices.text: Loading the warehouse
choices.why: It can read the same log once a night.

choices.text: Training a demand model
choices.why: The input is fixed; batch is cheaper.

choices.text: The stock shown on the website
choices.why: Right: a promise that depends on now.

prompt: A stream's monthly bill is three times what messages × bytes × days × copies predicts. What does the lesson suggest looking for?

choices.text: A broker bug that writes everything three times
choices.why: Replication is already in the arithmetic; look for what is not.

choices.text: Something else growing: unused partitions, unread groups, unchosen retention
choices.why: Right: the gap is a list of defaults nobody looked at.

choices.text: Compression that is too strong
choices.why: Stronger compression lowers storage, it does not triple it.

choices.text: Nothing; bills are always higher than arithmetic
choices.why: The point of the arithmetic is to make the gap visible.

prompt: Put the steps of sizing a new topic's disk in order.
items: Write a known number of real messages into an empty topic
Divide the size kafka-log-dirs.sh reports by that number
Multiply by messages a day, days kept and copies
Add room, and set retention.ms on the topic

prompt: Uncompressed, a sale took 135.3 bytes; with zstd, 16.9. About how many times smaller is the zstd topic? Answer to one decimal place.
